---
title: "Naive gene screen"
---

## Building $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ {#sec-fs-naive}

This chapter builds a working universe $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ on which a GGM
can be estimated. Genes are scored from one labelled single-cell
reference, used as a **signature**, not from a multi-sample atlas.
Global ranks (highly variable genes) and a short knowledge-driven marker
list both remove genes from the whole transcriptome. The all-versus-all
refinement that uses $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ comes **after** GRN
inference (@sec-fs-advanced).

Notation: gene $g=1,\ldots,G$; cell type $j=1,\ldots,J$; cell
$c=1,\ldots,C$. A cell labelled as type $j$ is written $c_{j}$. Bulk
samples stay indexed by $i$, as in the article. The DeCovarT convolution
is linear in $\boldsymbol{p}$ only on an additive scale
(@nte-linear-scale).

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-fs-naive
%%| fig-cap: "Naive screen on one labelled single-cell reference: Pearson-residual ranking and a short knowledge-driven marker list. No DESeq2 p-values."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["UMI y_cg, labels j"] --> B["Technical NB null, library size only"]
  B --> C["Pearson residuals r_cg"]
  C --> D["Rank by between versus within type"]
  E["Knowledge markers"] --> F["Gene universe G_0"]
  D --> F
  F --> G["GGM chapter"]
```

::: {#nte-linear-scale .callout-important}
## :warning: Keep the mixture on a linear scale

The convolution
$\boldsymbol{y}\mid(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p})\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$
is linear in $\boldsymbol{p}$ only if $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ live
on the **same additive scale** (counts, CPM, or TPM). Logarithms,
`SCTransform` Pearson residuals, and nonparanormal scores break that
map [@sturmComprehensiveEvaluationTranscriptomebased2019;
@jinBenchmarkRNAseqDeconvolution2021;
@hoffmannRobustComputationalReconstitution2006]. Use residualisation
only to **rank** genes; export DeCovarT moments on the linear scale.
The probabilistic reason is Jensen's inequality
(@nte-jensen-transform, @nte-npn-moments).
:::

## Highly variable genes as a signal-to-noise rank {#sec-fs-hvg}

Single-cell UMI tables mix depth noise with biological heterogeneity.
Regularised negative-binomial regression in `sctransform`
[@R-sctransform] / `Seurat::SCTransform` separates the two via Pearson
residuals [@hafemeisterNormalizationVarianceStabilization2019]. We use
that transform **only to rank genes**, not to normalise the table that
enters glasso or PLN, and not as a factorial arm of the GRN design
(@sec-grn-observation).

On this single-cell reference the only technical covariate we actually
have is **library size**. There is a single scRNA-seq resource, so
batch, donor and unmeasured technical branches cannot be identified
[@hafemeisterNormalizationVarianceStabilization2019]. The technical
null is therefore

$$
\log\mu_{cg}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\operatorname{offset}(\log L_{c}),
\qquad
y_{cg}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{cg},\theta_{g}),
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-null}

with $L_{c}$ the library size of cell $c$. **Do not** put cell type
$j$ in this null: that would remove the between-type signal the panel
is meant to keep.

Pearson residuals are

$$
r_{cg}
=
\frac{y_{cg}-\hat{\mu}_{cg}}
{\sqrt{\hat{\mu}_{cg}+\hat{\mu}_{cg}^{2}/\hat{\theta}_{g}}}.
$$ {#eq-fs-pearson}

@fig-sct-pearson recalls the NB mean–variance relation and the residual
scale used by `SCTransform`.

![`SCTransform` negative-binomial mean–variance relation and Pearson
residuals (Seurat v5).](images/scTransform_computation-1.png){#fig-sct-pearson}

### Total, biological, and technical pieces

For gene $g$ write $V_{\mathrm{total},g}=\mathrm{Var}_{c}(r_{cg})$ for
residual variation after the depth null. That leftover is **not** pure
biology: it still contains model misspecification. What we can split
with the labels $j$ is biological variation **between** versus
**within** cell types,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
C_{j}
\bigl(\bar{r}_{gj}-\bar{r}_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\bar{r}_{gj}
=
C_{j}^{-1}\sum_{c_{j}}r_{c_{j}g},\\
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
\sum_{c_{j}}
\bigl(r_{c_{j}g}-\bar{r}_{gj}\bigr)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fs-ss}

$C_{j}$ is the number of cells labelled $j$. Because the residuals are
globally approximately centred, $\bar{r}_{g}\approx 0$ and
$\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}\approx\sum_{j}C_{j}\bar{r}_{gj}^{2}$.
A lineage marker (high between-type, low within-type) is the gene we
want. A stress-response gene (low between-type, high within-type) is
not, even if its **total** residual variance is large.
@fig-pearson-sources sketches that split.

![Technical variation absorbed by a library-size negative-binomial null,
and biological residual variation split into between-type and
within-type pieces.](images/pearson_residual_variance_sources.png){#fig-pearson-sources}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-fs-varsplit
%%| fig-cap: "Residual variance after a library-size NB null. Technical variation is whatever the null absorbed; leftover variation is split into between-type and within-type biological pieces. Rank genes by a high between / low within ratio, not by total residual variance alone."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}}%%
flowchart TD
  Y["y_cg"] --> N["NB technical null: offset log L_c only"]
  N --> R["Pearson r_cg"]
  R --> T["Total residual variance"]
  T --> B["Between type"]
  T --> W["Within type"]
  B --> S["Keep high between, low within"]
  W --> S
```

There is **no** calibrated differential-expression $p$-value here: one
technical replicate cannot support `DESeq2` (@nte-pseudoreplication).
The between-type sum of squares is a **ranking score**.

Use `Seurat::SCTransform()` with Pearson residuals. That **is** the
residual transformation. Then **do not** stop at Seurat's default
variable features: those rank genes by **overall** residual variance,
which mixes within-type heterogeneity into the score.

After `SCTransform`, pull the residual matrix and compute
@eq-fs-ss by the labelled type $j$. Keep on the order of $2{,}000$
genes in $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ before any GGM
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008].

```{r}
#| label: sct-snr-rank
#| eval: false
# Sketch: Pearson residuals for ranking only; export counts to the GGM.
sct <- Seurat::SCTransform(
  seu,
  method = "glmGamPoi",
  residual.feature = NULL,
  return.only.var.genes = FALSE,
  vst.flavor = "v2"
)
R <- Seurat::GetAssayData(sct, assay = "SCT", layer = "scale.data")
# rows gene g, columns cell c; align with cell-type factor j
j <- sct$celltype
ss_between <- apply(R, 1, function(r) {
  means <- tapply(r, j, mean)
  n_j <- tapply(r, j, length)
  sum(n_j * means^2)
})
ss_within <- apply(R, 1, function(r) {
  sum(tapply(r, j, function(z) sum((z - mean(z))^2)))
})
snr <- ss_between / pmax(ss_within, .Machine$double.eps)
```

::: {#nte-hvg-not-gaussian .callout-note}
## :information_source: HVGs are not a GGM input

Pearson residuals are closer to homoscedastic than raw UMI counts,
which is why they are popular before PCA. They are still a **nonlinear
residualisation**. Feeding them indiscriminately into `SILGGM` silently
changes the estimand of $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ away from the latent
Gaussian that DeCovarT wants at the **population** level. If a Gaussian
GGM is used, prefer a copula / nonparanormal map on the same gene set
(@sec-silggm), or better a Poisson-lognormal latent Gaussian
(@sec-pln).
:::

## Marker genes {#sec-fs-markers}

Shannon entropy and Gini of relative means are compaction scores for
long one-versus-rest lists. Definitions live in the DeCovarT vignette
[supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd](https://github.com/bastienchassagnol/DeCovarT/blob/main/vignettes/supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd#L62-L254).

On this reference the marker list is **knowledge-driven** and already
short. It is stored as

`data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv`

with three columns: `cell_type_excel` (lineage name on the signalling
map), `cell_type_suppinger` (the matching Suppinger label, or `NA` when
that lineage is absent), and `gene_marker`. Because the list is a
curated biological seed rather than a concatenated differential-expression
shortlist, it does not by itself inflate collinearity of
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}$. Seeds may later be grown by Markov
boundaries (@sec-separation).

## Differential expression — only with biological replication {#sec-fs-deg}

`DESeq2`, `edgeR` and `limma`–voom remain the workhorses of
one-versus-rest ranking [@loveModeratedEstimationFold2014]. That logic
**does not transfer** to GSE229513 as a DE experiment.

::: {#nte-pseudoreplication .callout-warning}
## :warning: Technical pseudo-bulks are not biological replicates

Cells from a common experimental unit are not independent biological
replicates. Splitting or bootstrapping cells characterises
**technical / sampling** variability; it does not manufacture
between-organoid uncertainty. Treating cells, or random partitions of
cells, as `DESeq2` replicates inflates apparent degrees of freedom and
produces false discoveries [@squairConfrontingFalseDiscoveries2021;
@crowellMuscatDetectsSubpopulationspecific2020].

Use `DESeq2` in this book only if **independent biological replicates**
exist. For GSE229513, skip calibrated DE $p$-values. Rank genes by
@eq-fs-ss or by the knowledge table, not by a nested-model $F$ treated
as a $p$-value.

Bulk HTSeq tables (GSE229386) **do** have three biological replicates
per time and Wnt schedule (@sec-geo-design). Those replicates support
**bulk** DE of treatments, not cell-type GRNs from the scRNA-seq
object.
:::

## What we would actually run

1.  `SCTransform` Pearson residuals under @eq-fs-nb-null; rank by
    between/within @eq-fs-ss.
2.  Union with
    `data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv`
    (drop rows with `cell_type_suppinger` missing unless a later
    reference needs them).
3.  Cap $|\mathcal{G}_{0}|$ at a few thousand genes.
4.  **No** `DESeq2` $p$-values on technical sc pseudo-bulks.

## Perspectives: differential networks {#sec-fs-perspective}

These methods are **not** in the naive screen. They need graphs, so
they nominate extras for $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ **after** a first GGM pass.
Full algebraic detail of `INDEED` and D-trace lives in DeCovarT
`vignettes/supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd`. Separation language
(directed versus undirected) is in @sec-separation.

### Comparing supports, or estimating the difference {#sec-fs-diffnet}

DeCovarT benefits from **rewiring** between populations. A gene that
changes neighbourhood in $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ is a better candidate
than a gene that is merely highly variable.

**Fit every $\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$, then compare supports.** Independent
glasso / `SILGGM` fits (@sec-silggm) yield per-type edges; the symmetric
difference of supports ranks genes by differential connectivity. The
difference of two biased estimators is not a debiased estimator of
$\Delta_{j\ell}=\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}-\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\ell}$.

**Estimate $\Delta_{j\ell}$ directly.** D-trace methods target the
difference of precisions without necessarily reconstructing both graphs
first. Zhang and Zou [@zhangSparsePrecisionMatrix2014] introduced the
lasso-penalised D-trace loss for a single sparse precision; the
differential-network extension
[@yuanDifferentialNetworkAnalysis2017] estimates
$\Delta_{j\ell}$. Empirically, D-trace is competitive when the
**difference** is sparser than either graph
[@plaksienkoMethodsDifferentialNetwork2025]. It still does **not**
produce a pair of SPD precisions. A workable **proposal** is: use
D-trace to nominate rewiring genes, then estimate each
$\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}$ on that panel with a method from @sec-grn-top4.

### `INDEED`

`INDEED` multiplies a DE $p$-value by a permutation-filtered change in
partial correlation [@zuoINDEEDIntegratedDifferential2016]. On this
reference the DE $p$-value assumes biological replication
(@nte-pseudoreplication), and the permutation null among cells of one
gastruloid is a technical null. Use it, if at all, as a ranking
heuristic with $p_{g}^{\mathrm{DE}}$ replaced by a fold-change or
between-type score.

### Markov boundaries

Once a GGM exists, seeds (markers, high signal-to-noise genes, D-trace
hits) can be grown by undirected neighbours
$\{g':\theta_{gg'}\neq 0\}$. On a minimal undirected I-map that neighbour
set is the **Markov boundary**, the smallest Markov blanket
[@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988;
@kollerProbabilisticGraphicalModels2009]. That is undirected
separation, not DAG $d$-separation (@sec-separation,
@fig-separation).
